ai.definition: Cybersecurity threats refer to the various methods and techniques used by malicious actors to exploit vulnerabilities in computer systems, networks, and data. These threats can range from malware and phishing attacks to more sophisticated tactics like ransomware and zero-day exploits.
ai.howItWorks: Advanced encryption technologies work by converting plaintext into ciphertext using complex algorithms that are difficult for unauthorized users to decipher. Threat detection mechanisms use a combination of signature-based and behavioral analysis to identify potential security breaches in real-time.
ai.problemSolved: The rapid evolution of cyber threats necessitates robust protection strategies to safeguard sensitive data, maintain network integrity, and prevent unauthorized access or manipulation of systems.
ai.manufacturing: Manufacturing cybersecurity solutions involves developing software and hardware components that can effectively detect, prevent, and mitigate various types of attacks. This includes the creation of encryption algorithms, intrusion detection systems, and security protocols.
ai.buildProcess: The build process for cybersecurity technologies typically begins with research and development to identify emerging threats. This is followed by the design and implementation of protective measures, rigorous testing, and finally, deployment in real-world scenarios.
ai.costDrivers: Cost drivers include the complexity of developing advanced encryption algorithms, the continuous need for updates to adapt to new threats, and the high costs associated with maintaining a robust threat detection system.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: The outlook for cybersecurity technologies is positive as the demand for enhanced protection continues to grow. However, the rapid pace of technological change poses challenges in keeping up with emerging threats.
ai.regulation: Regulations vary by region but generally require organizations to implement certain security measures and report data breaches. Compliance often drives investment in cybersecurity solutions.
ai.risks: Risks include the potential for false positives or negatives in threat detection, the possibility of vulnerabilities being exploited before patches are developed, and the challenge of keeping up with rapidly evolving threats.
ai.profitability: Profitability is high due to the critical nature of cybersecurity services, but margins can be thin due to the need for continuous innovation and compliance costs.
ai.futureDevelopment: Future development will likely focus on integrating artificial intelligence and machine learning to enhance threat detection capabilities, improving user authentication methods, and developing more resilient encryption standards.

glossary.def: Software designed to harm a computer system or network, including viruses, worms, and Trojans.
A social engineering tactic where attackers use deceptive emails or messages to trick individuals into revealing sensitive information.
Malicious software that encrypts a victim's data and demands payment in exchange for the decryption key.
An attack on software, hardware, or firmware using a previously unknown vulnerability before a patch is available.

subsystems.name: Cryptographic core
subsystems.role: keeps data unreadable to anyone without keys, in transit and at rest.
parts: public-key algorithms for key exchange and signatures
hardware security modules and trusted platform modules

subsystems.name: Identity and access
subsystems.role: decides who and what may reach a system, and proves it.

subsystems.name: Network defence
subsystems.role: filters, segments and inspects traffic so one breach does not become many.

subsystems.name: Endpoint telemetry and control
subsystems.role: watches each device closely enough to spot and stop an attacker on it.
parts: kernel-level sensors (for example eBPF on Linux)

subsystems.name: Detection and analytics
subsystems.role: turns millions of raw events into a short list of things worth a human looking at.
parts: detection rules mapped to attacker tactics (e.g. MITRE ATT&CK)

subsystems.name: Response orchestration
subsystems.role: acts on a detection quickly and repeatably.
parts: integrations into firewalls, identity and endpoint tools

subsystems.name: Software and supply-chain integrity
subsystems.role: stops trusted software channels being used against you.

buildSteps.title: Map what you are defending
buildSteps.detail: Inventory devices, services, data stores and the flows between them; you cannot protect or instrument what you have not recorded.

buildSteps.title: Establish trust anchors
buildSteps.detail: Stand up certificate authorities and hardware key stores; issue device and service identities; retire shared passwords and unmanaged keys.

buildSteps.title: Harden and segment
buildSteps.detail: Remove unused services, apply least-privilege permissions, and cut the network into zones so lateral movement is slow and noisy.

buildSteps.title: Instrument everywhere
buildSteps.detail: Deploy endpoint sensors and central log collection; synchronise clocks and standardise event fields so records can be correlated.

buildSteps.title: Write detections, then try to beat them
buildSteps.detail: Encode known attack patterns as rules, map them to tactics, and have a red team attempt those same techniques to see what is missed.

buildSteps.title: Add behavioural analytics
buildSteps.detail: Train models on normal activity baselines, add them alongside rules, and tune thresholds until alert volumes are workable.

buildSteps.title: Automate the first response
buildSteps.detail: Build playbooks that isolate a host, revoke a token or block an address automatically, with human approval for disruptive actions.

buildSteps.title: Rehearse failure
buildSteps.detail: Test backups by restoring them, run incident exercises, and write post-incident reviews that change the rules.

buildSteps.title: Iterate continuously
buildSteps.detail: Patch on a schedule, refresh threat intelligence, and re-run detection tests as infrastructure changes.

prerequisites.why: everything else — identity, encryption, code signing — rests on ciphers and protocols that have survived decades of attack.
correlating events across systems is impossible if clocks or record formats disagree.

prerequisites.tech: Labelled attack data and threat intelligence
prerequisites.why: models and rules need examples of real intrusions, which defenders rarely have in quantity.

prerequisites.tech: Machine learning with tolerable false-positive rates
prerequisites.why: detection models work, but noisy alerts make analysts ignore real incidents.
most severe exploitable bugs are memory-safety errors, still pervasive in operating systems and network stacks.
secure boot and sealed key storage let a device prove it has not been tampered with.

pathway.milestone: layered perimeter, endpoint and log monitoring with multi-factor authentication
pathway.unlocks: detection of common intrusion techniques and quick containment of known threats.

pathway.milestone: zero-trust architectures with strong device identity and phishing-resistant authentication
pathway.unlocks: damage limitation even after credentials are stolen.

pathway.milestone: memory-safe rewrites of exposed services and software bills of materials across supply chains
pathway.unlocks: far fewer remotely exploitable flaws to patch.

pathway.milestone: migration to post-quantum cryptography as standards settle and hardware supports it
pathway.unlocks: protection against adversaries recording encrypted traffic now to decrypt later.
